title: The Town's Books
subtitle: Monday 30 September to Sunday 6 October 1974: A Newspaper with a Year Cut Out, a Hose in Winona, Seventy Stones and the Book in the Safe

setting.name: Linden Falls, Madison, Winona, the Old Union Church and the co-op, 30 September to 6 October 1974
setting.description: The research week. The party knows that Dawn is alive and kept, that travelers vanish every harvest, and that something in the Hollow keeps the town's luck. Now they need to know what it is and what it wants, and the town's records will tell them, if they can get at them. The Hollow Fork Furrow's bound volumes in the village hall go from 1903 to 1974 with 1904 neatly razored out; but the co-op sent every issue to the State Historical Society in Madison, which has it on microfilm, and the Linden Falls Courier, over the ridge, covered the first Harvest Supper from the other side. Rev. Caspar Penrose, the minister who refused the bargain in 1904, wrote everything in the Union Church register and hid it under the pulpit floor of the church at the head of the Hollow. The family that left, the Aldahls, are in Winona, across the Mississippi: Einar Aldahl, seventy-nine, who drove the 1951 guest over the Fork bridge and has never crossed back. The federal farm offices in Linden Falls have the watershed map and the crop-hail adjuster's records. And the Book itself, the back half of the co-op's 1903 minute ledger, is in the green Diebold safe in Harald Haugen's office, and the back room of the co-op holds seventy years of guests' luggage. Meanwhile the town moves from Concerned to Watchful: the sheriff comes to tell them there is no case, the co-op's night man follows them, and on Thursday 26 September (already passed) the board pencilled an alternate name under Dawn's.
setting.atmosphere: Paper and dust and microfilm whirr, county offices with linoleum floors and fluorescent lights, a Mississippi bridge, a trailer with a hose across its step, a sagging church in the dark with seventy stones behind it, a co-op office at night with a safe ticking as it cools, and a back room of suitcases. Most of this week happens in daylight and in public; let the dread come from what the paper says. Then the co-op after dark, and the truth of it (DC 20), and Dawn on the step of the hired man's house, saying she is fine.

keyLocations.name: Linden Falls: the courthouse square
keyLocations.description: The Kinnick County seat, 3,800 people, eighteen miles east over the watershed ridge, where the corn is black. A limestone courthouse of 1896 with the sheriff's office and jail in the basement; the Kinnick County Library, a Carnegie building, with the Linden Falls Courier on microfilm back to 1889; the federal building with the county ASCS office (crop programs, aerial photographs, acreage maps) and the Soil Conservation Service (watershed and soil maps); a Ben Franklin, a Rexall, a Hardee's out on the highway; and the Kinnick Mutual crop-hail adjuster's office over the hardware store.
features: The sheriff's office: Sheriff Clifford Dahlquist's missing-persons drawer, a file per name, each with a Hollow Fork motel register photostat and a La Crosse bus-depot parking ticket
The library microfilm reader in the reference room, and a librarian, Mrs. Jean Hovland, who has been waiting thirty years for someone to ask about Hollow Fork
The SCS office's wall map of the Hollow Fork Creek watershed, outlined in red
The hail adjuster's office: seventy years of Kinnick Mutual claim maps
encounters: Sheriff Clifford Dahlquist, 61, and Deputy Wes Garnett, 32
Mrs. Jean Hovland, 64, county librarian
Dale Severson, 50, Kinnick Mutual's hail adjuster, who has been paid nothing by Hollow Fork in thirty years and wonders why they keep paying premiums
secrets: CLUE A3 confirmed and A1 extended (core, from the sheriff's files; Persuasion DC 12 with Dahlquist, or automatic with Deputy Garnett's help): eleven files since 1954, each a traveler last seen in Hollow Fork, each with a motel register photostat reading 'checked out', each with a car found at the La Crosse Greyhound depot. Dr. Gessler's car had his bow case in the trunk. Dahlquist filed them all as adults who left of their own accord, which is what the evidence says. Deputy Garnett has been keeping a list of his own.

CLUE 1b, the Courier (core, automatic for anyone who reads October 1904 on the library microfilm; Research DC 12 to find it in under an hour): 'ROCKFORD MAN MISSING. Mr. Emmett Tilley, agent for the Rockford Seed Co., who attended the first Harvest Supper at Hollow Fork on Saturday last, has not returned to his hotel at Linden Falls. The Hollow Fork men say he departed on the evening stage. The stage driver says he did not.' Two weeks later, a letter to the editor from Rev. J. Penrose of the Union Church, Hollow Fork Township: 'There are bargains that cost more than they pay. I would not bless that table, and I will not stay to see what is set on it. Let those who have eaten there look to their names.' He resigned his pulpit in March 1905.

CLUE 2b (core, from the SCS watershed map laid over the hail adjuster's claim maps; either office will do the overlay for a polite request; Research DC 10, or Nature DC 10): seventy years of hail claims, plotted, stop exactly on the red watershed line. Dale Severson: 'Not one Hollow Fork claim since nineteen-oh-five. I've got hail paths on this map that come up the valley a mile wide and split around that watershed like water round a rock. I put it in a report in 1961. They told me to stop writing reports.'

keyLocations.name: The State Historical Society, Madison
keyLocations.description: Three hours east, on the University of Wisconsin campus at the end of State Street, the State Historical Society's great stone library holds one of the largest newspaper collections in the country, including the Hollow Fork Furrow, every issue since 1903, sent by the co-op as its first secretary, Gunnar Haugen, promised in a letter of 1903, and forgotten. The microfilm reading room is quiet, warm and full of graduate students, one of whom, Yolanda Ibarra, has been here before.
features: Reel 1 of the Furrow: January 1903 to December 1906
The Furrow's masthead: PUBLISHED BY THE HOLLOW FORK FARMERS' COOPERATIVE — G. HAUGEN, SEC'Y
A photostat machine at ten cents a page
encounters: A reference librarian; graduate students; nobody from Hollow Fork, which is why it matters
secrets: CLUE 1b, the Furrow (core, for anyone who reads the October 1904 issues): the issue of 6 October 1904 announces the first Harvest Days and 'by resolution of the Cooperative Board, every traveler in the township on the evening of 15 October will be welcome at the Harvest Supper table, without charge, and is urged to partake of the new bread baked from this year's Hollow Fork wheat'. The issue of 20 October: 'The Supper was a great success. Mr. E. Tilley of Rockford, Ill., guest of honour, departed on the evening stage.' The issue of 27 August 1904 has a single line in the Cooperative Notes: 'The Board met in special session on the night of the 24th, all seven members present, and concluded an agreement for the good of the township.'

A photograph on the front page of 20 October 1904: the seven board members at the Harvest Supper, with the guest of honour, a cheerful young man with a moustache, between them. Compared with Signe Aldahl's photograph (CLUE 4e) in Sylvie's handbag: the same seven men, the same week, the same red kerchiefs. Fear check DC 10 for anyone who looks at Emmett Tilley's smiling face and knows.

keyLocations.name: Einar Aldahl's trailer, Winona, Minnesota
keyLocations.description: An hour and a half west, over the Mississippi on the high bridge at Winona, in a trailer park on the Minnesota side below the bluffs, an aluminum Pacemaker trailer with a green awning, a tidy patch of tomatoes, a lawn chair facing the river, and a garden hose running from the spigot across the trailer's one step and down into the grass, on, all day and all night, the year round, with a heat tape wrapped round it for the winter. Einar Aldahl, seventy-nine, Signe Aldahl's brother-in-law and Sylvie's great-uncle, has lived here since 1952. He worked thirty years at a Winona box factory. He has not crossed the river since the night he crossed it.
features: A red kerchief, faded pink, hanging on a nail inside the door
A photograph of the Aldahl farm in Hollow Fork in 1950, the year before, on the wall: a white house, a red barn, cornfields to the rim of the Hollow (it is the Fossum place now)
encounters: Einar Aldahl, 79, small, bald, bright-eyed, with a cane and a temper, who has been expecting someone to come for twenty-three years
secrets: CLUE 1c (core, for anyone who talks to him honestly; he talks at once to Sylvie Aldahl): 'Don't eat their bread. If you've eaten their bread, you're a guest. If your name's in the Book, you're the guest. That's how it is and that's how it always was.'

CLUE 2d and 2c (core): the story of 1951. 'My dad was head of the house then, eighty-one years old. The board wrote the name, a nice young fellow from Chicago selling encyclopedias, Stan Wachowski, and Dad said no, not this time, and that night I put Stan in the back of my Hudson and drove him over the Fork bridge with every man in town on the road behind us, and the frost come down the corn after us like a white dog and stopped at the water. Stopped dead. Stan got out on the far bank and was sick and walked to Linden Falls and I never heard of him again. And that winter it walked. Every night. Hollow Fork lost its corn that year, the only year, and in the spring they made us sell to Per Fossum's boy and go. So I came over the big water, and I keep a hose on the step, and I never went back.'

CLUE 4c (core, for anyone who asks how it ends): 'Dad said there were two doors out, and they both cost. One is every house together, all seven, at the hole where they made it, and read it back. That's the one nobody'll ever do, because they'd lose everything. The other is the one that writes the names goes down instead. That's the one my dad thought about, and didn't, because it wasn't him that wrote them.'
Einar is the head of the house of Aldahl, and the Aldahls are one of the seven. He knows it. He will not go back over the river. In hs-scenario-004 he may.

keyLocations.name: The Old Union Church and the Seventy Stones
keyLocations.description: At the head of the Hollow, on a bench of land reached by a farm track from the Vaage place or a footpath along the rim, the Union Church of 1878: frame, grey, the steeple leaning, the door padlocked by the township in 1938, the windows boarded. Inside, pews under dust, a pump organ, a pulpit on a low platform, a stove, wasps. Behind it, the first settlers' cemetery, mown, and along its back fence a row of seventy-one small fieldstones set in the grass, each the size of a loaf of bread, with no names. Below the church, the cold slope and the Cold Hole. The cold flows up into the churchyard at dusk. Getting the padlock off is easy (Mechanics DC 10, or a crowbar); getting in without the town knowing is harder.
features: The pulpit platform: one board, newer than the others, with a nail-hole where a nail has been pulled and put back
The stones: one has been set this year, still raw, the grass not grown back; next to it, a space
A smell of cold stone and wet leaves through the floorboards
encounters: A Shade (Shade stats): the cold echo of a guest, Emmett Tilley, who sits in the front pew in his good suit with his hat on his knee, as if the supper were still to come. It is not hostile unless the register is taken; then it rises and follows the one who has it to the edge of the churchyard, whispering 'Is it time? Is it time?', and a fear check DC 15
Ingeborg Vaage, if it is a Wednesday or Sunday afternoon: she comes to mow round the stones
secrets: THE REGISTER (core, under the newer pulpit board, in a tin document box wrapped in oilcloth): the Union Church register, 1878 to 1905, in Rev. Caspar Penrose's neat hand. The last pages are his account of August to October 1904. CLUE 1d: 'Halvor Vaage came to me on the morning of the 25th and told me what they had agreed. One guest each harvest: a stranger who has eaten of their bread and whose name is written in their Book.' CLUE 3b: 'The Brandvold girl, Kari, nineteen, who was in the Vaage field after the cattle that night, says it came up the rows toward her like a white mist that breathed, and she lay down in the furrow with her face in the earth and held her breath, and it passed her by; she says it cannot see, and seeks the breath.' CLUE 2 (support): 'Halvor says it cannot go over running water nor beyond the ridges where the township's water runs.' CLUE 4b: 'It is a lease, and they spoke it as a lease. It is to be surrendered by every house that signed it, at the place where it was made, reading back their own names; or it is to be paid out by the hand that writes the names going down in the guest's stead. Halvor told me this as if it were a comfort.' And the last entry, 16 October 1904: 'Mr. Tilley did not take the stage. God forgive this township. I cannot.'

THE STONES (core, for anyone who counts them, a fear check DC 15; or who asks Ingeborg): seventy-one: seventy for the guests, and one, raw, for this year's. Ingeborg set them, one every year since 1904 (her father set the first ones; she has done it since 1931). This year's stone is already set. The space beside it is for 1975.

The Thin Place inside the church: shame, old and cold, and under it one man's fury, still warm after seventy years. Outside, among the stones: nothing. Whatever the guests feel, it is not here; they are down in the cold.

keyLocations.name: The Co-op Office and the Back Room
keyLocations.description: The Hollow Fork Farmers' Cooperative office on Main Street: a front counter, three desks, a calendar from the Madison bank, a framed photograph of the 1903 founding board (seven men), and behind Harald Haugen's desk the green Diebold safe of 1903, gold scrollwork, a combination dial and a brass handle. Behind the office a door marked STORAGE opens on a long windowless room under the feed mill, piled to the ceiling, and a back stair goes down to a basement full of rats and old seed sacks. The co-op closes at six. The night man, Vernon Kittleson, walks the elevator, the mill and the office on the hour with a flashlight and a CB until six in the morning, and reports to Harald on channel 14.
features: The Diebold safe: combination lock; Rolf Haugen has known the combination (his mother's birthday) since he was fourteen
The back room: seventy years of luggage
The co-op's base-station CB on the elevator's top floor, the flat voice that closes channel 14
encounters: Vernon Kittleson, 58, the night man (Night Watchman stats), who would rather not hurt anyone and will call for Arnie on channel 14 before he swings his flashlight
A Rat Swarm in the basement, if anyone goes down there
secrets: CLUE A4 (core, for anyone who opens the back room; THE TRUTH OF IT, fear check DC 20, DC 18 if they already know Rule One): luggage, floor to ceiling, in the order it came. At the front, a green Army knapsack with a peace sign drawn on it and a Polaroid SX-70 inside: Dawn's. Behind it, a canvas bow case and a hunting vest with a license pinned to it, GESSLER, HOWARD, 1973. Behind that, a guitar case; a blue hard-shell suitcase; then, unexpectedly, a gap on the shelf where a tag reading 1951 hangs from a nail with nothing under it, because Stan Wachowski's sample case went over the Fork bridge with him; then two bags tagged 1952; a 1940s hatbox; an Army duffel from 1946; a cardboard suitcase tied with rope; a carpetbag; and at the very back, under seventy years of dust, a leather seed-sample case stamped ROCKFORD SEED CO. — E. TILLEY. Every one has a manila tag on the handle in a co-op clerk's hand: a year.

CLUE B5 (core, in Dawn's knapsack): a stack of Polaroids. Main Street, smiling townsfolk with their arms around her, Elsie, the elevator, the Harvest Moon, the corn; then the Fossum yard; the hired man's house; Lillian at the stove; Dawn asleep in a chair; and the last one, dated in Dawn's hand on the white border '9/20 — so tired — so happy?', a picture of the inside of the hired man's house window at night, white with frost, except for a round clear patch.

THE BOOK (core, in the safe): the back half of the co-op's 1903 minute ledger, a heavy book bound in green cloth and red leather corners. CLUE 4a: its first page, in Gunnar Haugen's copperplate, headed THE AGREEMENT OF 24TH AUGUST 1904, gives the terms (as in campaignRules, The Landlord's Rules) and seven signatures, one per line, each with a house name: VAAGE, HAUGEN, BRANDVOLD, KUBICEK, LUNDE, FOSSUM, ALDAHL. CLUE 1a: then seventy lines, one a year, each a date, a name, a home town, 'took supper' and a date, and 'Paid'. 1951: 'S. Wachowski, Chicago — UNPAID — went over the water.' 1952: two names. 1973: 'Dr. H. Gessler, Evanston Ill. — took supper 10/2/73 — Paid.' 1974, in ink, dated 2 September: 'Dawn Petrakis, Rockford Ill.', the 'took supper' left blank for the Harvest Supper. And under it, in pencil, dated 26 September: 'alt. — R. Thorsen, Vilas Co.' (or whichever outsider has eaten most; GM's choice).

Harald's handwriting: the entries since 1955 are his. The pencil is his. The minutes of the Labor Day board meeting, in the front half of the same ledger, record only 'The Board met; all six members present; the annual business was concluded.'

keyLocations.name: The Hired Man's House at the Fossum Place
keyLocations.description: A small white frame house across the Fossum farmyard from the main house: a kitchen, a front room, a bedroom, curtains drawn, a hose running across the front step and another across the back, a red kerchief on the doorknob. Lillian keeps it warm and clean. Dawn sleeps a great deal, eats everything Lillian brings her, smokes on the step in the afternoon, and does not want to go anywhere.
features: The kitchen: a bread box always full of Arvid's bread, a pot of soup always on
Dr. Kubicek's bottle of 'tonic' on the windowsill: it is vitamins and a little phenobarbital, which keeps her drowsy; Tess or any Physician identifies it at once (Medicine DC 10)
The bedroom window: frost on the inside every night
encounters: Dawn Petrakis, 22, content and slow
Lillian Fossum, 46, who is there from seven in the morning to nine at night
The two farm dogs; Arnie and his sons in the barn at milking (five to seven, morning and evening)
secrets: Dawn (core): she is fine, she says, really fine, the people are so nice, she is staying for the festival, Mrs. F needs her. She is under the pull (Rule One) at its deepest after a month of the town's bread; she will not leave of her own will. Insight DC 10: under the contentment she is frightened and does not know why. Tess saying her name, and the name of home, and something only the two of them know, gives her a WIS save DC 15 to want to leave; each further day without the town's bread gives another save with advantage.

Lillian (core, Insight DC 12, then kindness): she will cry, and tell the party that she was born in Linden Falls, married in, and has been afraid every Labor Day for twenty-four years that the board would write her name; that she looks after the guests because someone should be kind to them; that she has never told anyone that she prays every night for the Hollow to freeze solid. She will not betray Arnie. She will leave a door unlocked.

synopsis: The party digs into the town's records while the town watches them do it. Over the ridge in Linden Falls the sheriff shows them eleven missing-persons files, every one closed, and Deputy Wes Garnett, who has been keeping his own list, becomes an ally; the county library's microfilm of the Linden Falls Courier has 'ROCKFORD MAN MISSING' from October 1904 and a letter from the Union Church's minister refusing to bless 'that table'; the federal farm offices' watershed map lies exactly over seventy years of hail claims that stop at the ridge. In Madison the State Historical Society's microfilm of the Hollow Fork Furrow, the co-op's own paper, has the 1904 issues the village hall razored out: the first Harvest Supper, every traveler welcome, the new bread, and Mr. Tilley 'departed on the evening stage'. In Winona, across the Mississippi, Einar Aldahl of the family that left tells them what he did in 1951, what the bread means, why there is a hose across his step, and that there are two ways out and both cost. At the Old Union Church at the head of the Hollow they find Rev. Penrose's register under the pulpit, with the whole of the bargain as it was spoken in 1904, and behind the church seventy fieldstones, one for each guest. Finally, with or without Rolf Haugen's help, they get into the co-op after dark: the back room is seventy years of guests' luggage, Dawn's knapsack at the front, and the safe holds the Book, its first page the lease with seven signatures, its seventy lines the names, and under Dawn's name, in pencil, one of their own. The scenario ends when they find Dawn at the Fossums' hired man's house, safe, kindly kept and unwilling to leave, and must decide how to get her out.
hook: Monday 30 September. Twelve days to Harvest Days. The party has seen the cold on Main Street and knows Dawn is at the Fossum place. Quentin's editor wants copy; Yolanda's advisor wants a chapter; Russ has a name for the thing he is hunting. Each of the leads is a place they can go: Linden Falls, Madison, Winona, the church at the head of the Hollow, the co-op. The town, now Concerned, would very much like them to stay in Hollow Fork, and offers them all something to do this week.

conclusions.conclusion: RULE ONE. It may take only a guest: an outsider fed on Hollow Fork bread whose name is written in the Book
clues: 1a: the Book's seventy lines, every name from out of town, every one 'took supper' (the co-op safe)
1b: the Furrow of October 1904, every traveler welcome at the table and urged to eat the new bread, against the Courier's ROCKFORD MAN MISSING (Madison; Linden Falls)
1c: Einar Aldahl: 'If your name's in the Book, you're the guest' (Winona)
1d: Rev. Penrose's register: 'a stranger who has eaten of their bread and whose name is written' (the Old Union Church)
A4: the guests' luggage in the co-op back room, tagged by year

conclusions.conclusion: RULE TWO. It cannot cross running water, or go beyond the land that drains into the Hollow
clues: 2b: the watershed map laid over seventy years of hail claims (Linden Falls)
2d: the Book's 1951 line, 'UNPAID — went over the water', and Einar's story of the Fork bridge (the co-op safe; Winona)
2c: Einar's hose across his trailer step on the far side of the Mississippi (Winona); the hoses in Hollow Fork (hs-scenario-001)
Rev. Penrose's register: 'it cannot go over running water nor beyond the ridges where the township's water runs' (the Old Union Church)
2a: the frost line of 23 September (hs-scenario-001)

conclusions.conclusion: RULE THREE. It is blind and hunts by breath; a hidden breath is passed by
clues: 3b: Kari Brandvold in the furrow, 1904, in Rev. Penrose's register (the Old Union Church)
3a: frost reaching for the sleeper's breath (hs-scenario-001), and Dawn's last Polaroid of the frosted window with its clear patch (the co-op back room)
3c: the wetted kerchiefs (hs-scenario-001)
3d: Ingeborg Vaage, if they ask her straight this week: 'It can't see, child. It listens for your breath'

conclusions.conclusion: RULE FOUR. The bargain is a lease: surrendered by all seven houses at the Cold Hole, or paid out by the hand that writes the names
clues: 4a: the Book's first page, the terms and seven signatures (the co-op safe)
4b: Rev. Penrose's register, 'It is a lease, and they spoke it as a lease' (the Old Union Church)
4c: Einar Aldahl, 'two doors out, and they both cost' (Winona)
4e: Signe Aldahl's photograph of the seven, matched with the Furrow's front page (Sylvie's handbag; Madison)

conclusions.conclusion: Dawn is at the Fossum place, kept drowsy and content, and someone else's name is pencilled under hers
clues: B5: Dawn's Polaroids in her knapsack, the last ones at the Fossum place (the co-op back room)
The Book: Dawn's name in ink, the alternate in pencil (the co-op safe)
Lillian's Kools and the hired man's house (hs-scenario-001), and Rolf Haugen, who will tell them outright
Dr. Kubicek's 'tonic' on the windowsill (the hired man's house)

acts.title: Monday and Tuesday: Over the Ridge
acts.description: Linden Falls and Madison. The party leaves Hollow Fork for the first time and finds that over the ridge the corn is black and the people are ordinary, and that the county knows something is odd about Hollow Fork in the way a county knows things it never says. The point of this act is the outside record: the sheriff's files, the Courier, the watershed and hail maps, and the Furrow on microfilm. It also gives the party a lawman ally, Deputy Wes Garnett, and shows them that the law will not help without evidence that would stand up in Linden Falls, which talk of the Hollow will not.
objectives: See the sheriff's missing-persons files and recruit Deputy Wes Garnett
Read the Linden Falls Courier for October 1904 at the county library
Lay the watershed map over the hail claims at the farm offices
Read the Hollow Fork Furrow for 1904 on microfilm in Madison (optional, a full day)

scenes.name: The Sheriff's Drawer
scenes.description: Sheriff Clifford Dahlquist, 61, is tired, decent, under-funded and twelve months from his pension, and he likes Hollow Fork, where the coffee is free and nobody ever calls him. He has a drawer of eleven missing-persons files since 1954 (A1, A3), and every one has the same three pieces of paper: a photostat of the Harvest Moon register reading 'checked out', a parking ticket or tow report from the La Crosse Greyhound depot, and a note from a relative. He filed them all as adults who left of their own accord. He will show the files to a polite party (Persuasion DC 12), and say there is no case, and that he is going out to Hollow Fork on Wednesday anyway for the co-op's coffee. Deputy Wes Garnett, 32, a farm boy from over the ridge and a bowhunter, has been keeping his own list in a spiral notebook since Dr. Gessler went missing, because the doctor's car had a bow case in the trunk and no hunter leaves his bow. He will follow the party out to the parking lot. He is a companion from here on, if they want him, and he has a radio in his cruiser and a county badge, which counts for something until it doesn't.
scenes.readAloud: The sheriff's office is in the courthouse basement: green linoleum, a coffee maker, a police scanner muttering, two cells with their doors open and nobody in them, and a heavy man with a grey crew cut behind a steel desk, eating a sandwich out of waxed paper. "Hollow Fork," he says, when you tell him, and puts the sandwich down. "Nicest town in the county. Never any trouble." He opens the bottom drawer of a filing cabinet without getting up, as if he knew which drawer you wanted, and puts eleven manila folders on the desk. "People go missing from everywhere, folks. Adults have a right to go missing. Every one of these checked out of the motel and left their car at the bus station in La Crosse. Every one." He taps the stack. "I've looked. I want you to know I've looked." Behind him, by the coffee maker, a young deputy in a tan uniform has stopped pretending to read the paper.

skillChecks.success: Laid side by side, the eleven files are the same file: the same motel, the same handwriting on the 'checked out', the same bus depot, the same window of dates, 8 to 20 September for the register and early to mid October for the car turning up at the depot. And in none of them did anyone check whether a bus ticket was ever bought. Dr. Gessler's car had his bow case in the trunk. (A1, A3.)
skillChecks.failure: Eleven sad little files. People do go missing. The sheriff wants his lunch.

skillChecks.success: Dahlquist rubs his face and says: 'Look. I'm not saying there's nothing. I'm saying I can't take a feeling to the district attorney. You bring me something a jury would look at, a body, a confession, a piece of paper, and I'll drive out there myself.' He means it. He will remember it in hs-scenario-004.
skillChecks.failure: 'Go home, folks. Or go to the festival, it's a good one. Elsie's pie.' He puts the files back in the drawer.

skillChecks.success: The deputy, Garnett, is angry and has been for a year. In the parking lot he hands you a spiral notebook with a list of names going back further than the sheriff's, from the county's old missing-persons index, to 1938, and says: 'I'm off at four. I've got a bow and a shotgun and a car with a radio. What do you need?'
skillChecks.failure: The deputy is reading the paper.

scenes.name: The Microfilm Reader
scenes.description: The Kinnick County Library, Linden Falls: a Carnegie building with a reference room, a microfilm reader that hums and smells of hot dust, and Mrs. Jean Hovland, 64, county librarian since 1944, who brings the Courier's 1904 reel without being told which one, because she has been waiting thirty years for someone to ask (CLUE 1b, the Courier). In Madison (a three-hour drive each way, or a long day) the State Historical Society has the Furrow itself (CLUE 1b, the Furrow, and the front-page photograph). Either is enough for Rule One's newspaper clue; both together make the case. The Courier also has, in October 1951, a two-line item: 'Chicago man walks into Linden Falls at dawn, says he was chased by Hollow Fork men. Declines to make a complaint.' Mrs. Hovland: 'My mother was from Hollow Fork. She married out. She never would eat at a Hollow Fork table again, not even Christmas. I always thought it was a feud.'
scenes.readAloud: The microfilm reader is a grey steel hood with a screen the size of a newspaper page, and when you wind the reel the past goes by in a blur of columns, ads for liniment and corsets and cream separators, grain prices, a church social, a fire. October 1904. LOCAL AND PERSONAL. A HARVEST SUPPER AT HOLLOW FORK. And under it, three paragraphs, small type: ROCKFORD MAN MISSING. Mr. Emmett Tilley, agent for the Rockford Seed Co., who attended the first Harvest Supper at Hollow Fork on Saturday last, has not returned to his hotel at Linden Falls. The Hollow Fork men say he departed on the evening stage. The stage driver says he did not. The librarian, who brought you the reel without asking which one you wanted, is standing behind you, reading it over your shoulder, with her hand at her throat.

skillChecks.success: You find it in twenty minutes, and keep going: two weeks later, Rev. Penrose's letter ('Let those who have eaten there look to their names'); in March 1905 his resignation; and in October 1951, the two lines about a Chicago man who walked into Linden Falls at dawn. In Madison, the Furrow gives you the other side: every traveler welcome at the table, the new bread, and Mr. Tilley departing on the evening stage, with his photograph. (CLUE 1b.)
skillChecks.failure: It takes all afternoon, and you find the missing-man story, and nothing else before the library closes at five. Mrs. Hovland says she'll pull the rest for you tomorrow.

skillChecks.success: Mrs. Hovland tells you about her mother, and the Christmases, and that there is an old saying over the ridge that nobody says in front of Hollow Fork people: 'Don't eat at the Fork in the fall.' She has never known what it meant. She thinks she does now.
skillChecks.failure: Mrs. Hovland is helpful and professional and keeps her thoughts to herself.

skillChecks.success: Compare the Furrow's front-page photograph of 20 October 1904 with Signe Aldahl's photograph from Sylvie's handbag: the same seven men, the same red kerchiefs, the same week; and the cheerful young man with the moustache in the middle of the Furrow's picture is not in Signe's. Signe's was taken after. On the back of hers, in pencil, the seven names, and 'the rim, 24 Aug. 1904, after'. (CLUE 4e.)
skillChecks.failure: Two old photographs of farmers in their Sunday clothes.

scenes.name: The Watershed Map
scenes.description: The federal building in Linden Falls: the county ASCS office (aerial photographs of every farm, flown every few years since 1938) and the Soil Conservation Service, whose wall map of the Hollow Fork Creek watershed is outlined in red. Over the hardware store, Dale Severson, the Kinnick Mutual hail adjuster, keeps seventy years of claim maps. Bring them together (CLUE 2b). The 1938 and 1951 aerial photographs show something else: in the 1951 photograph, flown in October after the frost, Hollow Fork's fields are black like everyone's. It is the only one.
scenes.readAloud: The adjuster unrolls his maps on the SCS office's big table, one on top of another, onionskin over onionskin, seventy years of hail: crayon tracks a mile wide coming up the coulees from the southwest, storm after storm, red, blue, green, a different colour every decade. The soil conservationist lays her watershed map over them, a red line looping round the Hollow Fork Creek basin like a fence round a pasture. For a moment nobody says anything. Every hail track in seventy years runs up to the red line, and splits, and goes round. Not one crosses it. "I wrote a report in 1961," the adjuster says. "They told me to stop writing reports."

skillChecks.success: There is no natural reason for it: hail does not follow watersheds; it follows storms. Whatever bounds Hollow Fork's luck is the land that drains into the Hollow, and nothing else, and it has been for seventy years. (CLUE 2b.)
skillChecks.failure: A striking pattern. You are not sure what it means about anything.

skillChecks.success: In the ASCS aerial photographs, Hollow Fork is green every October since 1938, except October 1951, when its corn is as black as everyone's and there is a line of cars stopped on the Fork bridge in the picture, flown the morning after something.
skillChecks.failure: The photographs are a lot of farms from the air.

skillChecks.success: Dale Severson has been frightened of Hollow Fork for thirteen years and has never told anyone. He tells you that Marit Lunde, the banker, called his boss in 1961 to have his report withdrawn, and that the co-op has paid Kinnick Mutual a premium every year since 1905 for hail insurance it has never once claimed.
skillChecks.failure: The adjuster is a quiet man who likes maps.

encounters: None hostile. On the way back over the ridge each evening, a pickup with a CB whip follows the party from the divide into Hollow Fork at a polite distance: Vernon Kittleson, the co-op night man, or one of the Fossum boys, reporting on channel 14

acts.title: Wednesday and Thursday: The Family That Left
acts.description: Winona and the Old Union Church. The party hears the story of 1951 from the only man who ever broke the bargain, and finds the minister's account of 1904 in the church at the head of the Hollow. The point of this act is the rules as spoken, from the two people who said no, and the first time the party goes to the Hollow's edge on purpose. Meanwhile the sheriff visits Hollow Fork on Wednesday, has pie, and tells the party over the counter, in front of Elsie, that there is no case.
objectives: Find Einar Aldahl in Winona and hear the story of 1951
Get into the Old Union Church and find Rev. Penrose's register

scenes.name: A Hose Across the Step
scenes.description: Winona, Minnesota, across the Mississippi high bridge. Einar Aldahl's trailer, the hose running across the step. Einar, seventy-nine, is rude to strangers and opens up at once to Sylvie Aldahl ('You're Magnus's granddaughter. You've got Signe's eyes. Sit down') or to anyone who tells him truthfully what they have seen. He gives CLUES 1c, 2c, 2d and 4c, and the story of the Fork bridge. He has kept his father's red kerchief. He will not go back across the river: 'Not for you, not for God, not for Signe's girl.' Insight DC 12: he is ashamed of that, and the shame is the only thing that might move him later. If the party tells him the town has written another name, a living person's, he goes very quiet.
scenes.readAloud: The trailer sits under the bluffs in a row of trailers facing the river, an old aluminum Pacemaker with a green awning, a lawn chair and a patch of tomatoes gone over in the cold. A garden hose comes off the spigot at the corner, runs across the single concrete step, and goes down into the grass, and the water is running, and has been running so long it has worn a little channel in the lawn down toward the river. An old man opens the door before you knock: small, bald, eyes like a bird's, a cane in one hand. He looks at you, all of you, one by one, and then at the river behind you, wide and grey and moving. "Hollow Fork," he says. It isn't a question. "You've eaten their bread. I can see it on you." He stands aside. "Wipe your feet. Step over the water. Don't step on it, step over it, it don't like being stepped on."

skillChecks.success: Einar tells you everything he knows: the bread and the Book (1c), the night of the Fork bridge (2d), the hose (2c), and the two doors (4c). At the end he takes a faded red kerchief off a nail by the door and gives it to whichever of you he likes best. 'Wet it in the creek. Running water, mind, not a bucket. Over your mouth. It can't see you, it can only hear you breathing. My dad lay in the corn with his face in a furrow the night it walked for us, and it went right over him.' (3b support.)
skillChecks.failure: Einar tells you about the Fork bridge, because he has wanted to tell someone for twenty-three years, and then tells you to get out before you bring it over the river with you, which you can't, but he doesn't care.

skillChecks.success: Einar is not afraid of the thing in the Hollow, any more. He is afraid of going back and seeing that nothing he did mattered: that they just wrote two names the next year. He is the head of the house of Aldahl. He knows that, and he knows what it means, and that is why the hose has been running for twenty-three years.
skillChecks.failure: An old man who left a bad place and is not going back.

skillChecks.success: Everything Einar says fits together: rules, not malice. It is bound like a lease is bound; it keeps its terms exactly, and so it can be held to them. Whatever this thing is, it has no church and no worship and no story but this one, and it is not a spirit of the dead. It is something that makes bargains. (An Occultist may use Old Lore here for a rule the party lacks.)
skillChecks.failure: An old man's story. It sounds like a hundred folk tales, and like none of them.

scenes.name: The Old Union Church
scenes.description: The church at the head of the Hollow, reached by the farm track past Ingeborg's stone house or along the rim footpath (fifteen minutes from the Fossum lane; the town will see a car on Ingeborg's track, and Ingeborg will see anyone on foot and say nothing). The padlock (Mechanics DC 10 or a crowbar). Inside: dust, pews, a pump organ, a stove, wasps, a Shade in the front pew (Emmett Tilley, in his good suit, hat on his knee; fear check DC 15 on first seeing him). Under the newer pulpit board, the tin box and the register (CLUES 1d, 3b, 4b and Rule Two support). If the register is lifted out, Tilley's Shade rises and follows its holder to the edge of the churchyard whispering 'Is it time? Is it time? I was promised supper', and fades in daylight; it can be laid, briefly, by telling it truthfully that the supper is over and it can rest (Occult DC 13; a Chaplain's Graveside gives advantage), which lets the party go without it following. It is not a creature to fight: its Shade stats are for the party's panic, not its malice. Dusk at the church is a bad time: the cold flows up from the Hollow into the churchyard and the Cold Hole can be heard breathing.
scenes.readAloud: Inside, the church is grey light through the cracks in the boarded windows, and dust, and the smell of old hymnals and mice. Pews in two rows. A pump organ with its keys yellow as old teeth. A pot-bellied stove. A low platform at the front with a plain pulpit on it. And in the front pew, on the left, a man sitting very straight, with his back to you: a young man in a brown suit, his hair parted and oiled, his hat on his knee, as if he were waiting for something to begin. The dust on the pew beside him is undisturbed. You can see the pulpit through him. He turns his head, a little, as if he had heard you come in, and says, in a pleasant, hopeful, Illinois voice, "Is it time?"

skillChecks.success: One board of the pulpit platform is newer than the rest, and its nail has been pulled and pushed back by hand. Under it, in oilcloth, a tin document box, and in it the Union Church register, Rev. Penrose's neat hand to the last page. (CLUES 1d, 3b, 4b.)
skillChecks.failure: It takes you an hour, and dusk is coming, and the cold is coming up into the churchyard through the floor before you find the loose board.

skillChecks.success: You speak to the man in the brown suit, gently, by name: the supper is over, Mr. Tilley, it was a long time ago, you can rest. He looks at his hat. 'Is it over? They were so kind.' And he is not there. He will not follow the register. (A Chaplain's Graveside gives advantage.)
skillChecks.failure: He rises when you lift the box, and follows you, a step behind, whispering 'Is it time? I was promised supper,' to the churchyard fence, where the daylight takes him. Fear check DC 15 for whoever carries the box, if they have not already lost Dread to him this scene.

skillChecks.success: Through the cracks in the floorboards, from below: cold air, and a sound like breathing, very slow, coming up from the slope under the church. The Cold Hole is directly beneath the bench the church stands on. Penrose preached his last sermon standing on top of it.
skillChecks.failure: It is very cold in here for a sunny day.

scenes.name: Seventy Stones
scenes.description: Behind the church, the first settlers' cemetery and, along the back fence, the stones. Counting them is a fear check DC 15 for anyone who knows what they are. If it is Wednesday or Sunday afternoon, Ingeborg Vaage is there with a push mower and a cushion for her knees. She does not pretend. She has set a stone every year since 1931, and her father before her; this year's is set already, raw, and the space beside it is for next year. She gives CLUE 3d if asked how to hide from it, and if asked anything else says, 'Not here. Come to the house. Not this week. When you're ready to do something, come to the house, and I'll tell you all of it.' In hs-scenario-003 she does.
scenes.readAloud: They are just stones: fieldstones the size of a loaf of bread, grey and lichened at one end of the row and raw at the other, set in the grass in a straight line along the back fence of the churchyard, a foot apart, with no names. Somebody mows around them; the grass is neat, and someone has pulled the thistles. You count them without meaning to. Sixty-nine. Seventy. Seventy-one. The last one is new: the turf has been cut and put back around it and has not grown in yet. And beyond it, at the end of the row, a foot further on, the turf has been neatly cut in a square and left, as if to mark a place.

skillChecks.success: Ingeborg sits back on her heels and tells you: one for every guest; her father set them from 1904 and she has since he died; she knows every name. This one is Dr. Gessler (she touches the 1973 stone); this one is for the girl (the raw one). 'I set it the day they wrote her. I always do. So it's ready.' And then: 'It can't see, child. It listens for your breath. Remember that.' (CLUE 3d.)
skillChecks.failure: Ingeborg goes on mowing, and says, 'Not here. Come to the house when you're ready to do something.'

skillChecks.success: She wants it to end. She has wanted it to end for seventy years. She has never said so to anyone in Hollow Fork, because she is a Vaage, and her father made it, and her mother lived.
skillChecks.failure: An old woman tending graves.

skillChecks.success: There are no graves here. The turf under the stones has never been dug deeper than a hand. Whatever happened to the guests, they are not in this churchyard.
skillChecks.failure: A row of stones in a graveyard.

encounters: Emmett Tilley's Shade in the Old Union Church (Shade stats; fear check DC 15; better laid than fought)
A Crow Swarm on the rim path if anyone goes down toward the Cold Hole

At dusk in the churchyard, the cold flows up out of the Hollow; the Landlord does not leave the Hollow in daylight and does not hunt this week, but anyone in the churchyard after sunset hears it breathe, fear check DC 15

acts.title: Friday to Sunday: The Co-op After Dark
acts.description: The Book. The party gets into the co-op office and its back room after closing, with Rolf Haugen's help or without it, and finds the truth of the town: seventy years of luggage, and the Book. Then they go to the hired man's house and find Dawn, and Dawn does not want to leave. The point of this act is the party knowing all four rules, seeing their own name (or a friend's) in pencil under Dawn's, and understanding that the town will not let them simply take her: which is hs-scenario-003.
objectives: Win Rolf Haugen's help, or get past Vernon Kittleson and open the safe without it
See the back room and read the Book
Reach Dawn at the hired man's house and begin to bring her back to herself

scenes.name: Little Elevator
scenes.description: Rolf Haugen, 24, drives the co-op's grain truck, eats lunch alone in the cab, and talks on channel 14 as Little Elevator. He has known since he was sixteen what his father writes in the Book; his father told him, the night of his sixteenth birthday, because one day the pen will be his. He has never said a word. He will talk to the party (anyone who catches him alone and is straight with him, Persuasion DC 13; automatic if they show him a Polaroid of the back room, Dawn's last Polaroid, or the pencilled name) and, once he talks, he is a companion. He knows the safe combination (his mother's birthday, 4-11-21), Vernon Kittleson's rounds (the elevator on the hour, the mill at quarter past, the office at half past), and that his father sits in the office some nights with the Book open in front of him and doesn't write anything. 'He's not a bad man. He's not. I need you to understand that.'
scenes.readAloud: The co-op grain truck is parked at the edge of the elevator lot with its engine ticking, and the big fair-haired young man in the cab has a sandwich in his lap that he isn't eating. When you come up to the window he looks at you for a long time. "You're the ones who've been to Winona," he says. "Everybody knows. Vernon followed you to the bridge." He looks across the lot at the co-op office window, where his father's grey head is bent over his desk. "Dad wrote the girl's name on Labor Day. He's written one every year since before I was born." He says it flatly, like a man reading out a grain price. Then his face does something, and he puts both hands on the wheel. "Get in. Not here. Get in, and I'll drive."

skillChecks.success: Rolf drives you out the ridge road to the divide, where the corn is black on one side, and tells you: the board, the Labor Day meeting, the Book, the back room, the combination, Vernon's rounds. He will take you in tonight. And: 'There's a name in pencil under hers. Dad wrote it last week. I don't know whose. I didn't want to look.'
skillChecks.failure: Rolf says he can't. Not to his father. He drives away. But that night, at eleven, someone leaves the co-op office's back door off the latch, and Vernon's rounds go past it twice without checking.

skillChecks.success: Rolf is not afraid of the thing in the Hollow. He is afraid of the pen. If the bargain goes on, in ten years he will sit at that desk on Labor Day and write a stranger's name, and he would rather die. He has thought about leaving, and stayed, because his father is drowning.
skillChecks.failure: A young man under a lot of pressure. You aren't sure which way he'll jump.

skillChecks.success: If you would rather not trust Rolf: you get Vernon Kittleson away from the office for half an hour with a story on channel 14 (heifers on the road, a fire at the dryer, a stranger at the elevator). He goes, grumbling, and reports to Harald on the way, and Harald does not come.
skillChecks.failure: Vernon goes, and comes back too soon, and finds the office door open.

scenes.name: The Back Room and the Book
scenes.description: The co-op after dark. The office (the safe: with Rolf, it opens; without, Mechanics DC 18 and twenty minutes, or a crowbar and an hour and a lot of noise). The back room (CLUES A4 and B5; the truth of it, fear check DC 20, DC 18 with Rule One known). The Book (CLUES 4a, 1a, 2d, and the pencilled alternate; fear check DC 15 for the character whose name is pencilled, or the friend of the one). Vernon Kittleson's rounds (Night Watchman stats; he does not want to hurt anyone and will call channel 14 for Arnie at once; Arnie and four men arrive in six minutes). Taking the Book is possible, and the town will know by morning; Polaroids of every page are smarter. The Rat Swarm is in the basement. The scene's last beat: Harald Haugen, in his coat, standing in the office doorway, looking at the party with the Book open on his desk. He does not call anyone. He says: 'Put it back where it was, please. It's very old.' And then, to whoever has their name in pencil: 'I'm sorry. I'm so sorry.' And goes home.
scenes.readAloud: The back room is long and low and smells of dust and leather and old paper, and when the flashlight finds the far wall it does not find a wall. It finds luggage. Suitcases, stacked to the ceiling, row after row back into the dark: a green Army knapsack with a peace sign inked on its flap; a canvas bow case; a guitar case; a blue hard-shell suitcase; a salesman's case of brushes; a hatbox; an Army duffel; a cardboard suitcase tied with rope; a carpetbag; and somewhere at the very back, under a grey fur of dust, a leather case with brass corners. Every one has a manila tag on its handle. You lift the nearest. It says, in a clerk's neat hand, 1974. The next says 1973. You do not need to read the rest. You can see the dates going back into the dark like the rings of a tree.

skillChecks.success: The Book, read properly: the terms on the first page in Gunnar Haugen's hand; seven signatures and seven house names; seventy lines; 1951 UNPAID; 1952 two names; nineteen lines in Harald's hand since 1955; Dawn's name in ink; and in pencil beneath it, dated 26 September, 'alt.' and a name you know. Photograph every page. (CLUES 4a, 1a, 2d.)
skillChecks.failure: You read the first page and the last lines, and hear Vernon's boots on the mill stair, and have to close the Book before you have read the rest.

skillChecks.success: Vernon's flashlight passes the office window and goes on to the mill. You have twenty minutes.
skillChecks.failure: Vernon's flashlight stops on the office window. 'Who's in there?' He keys his CB. 'Big Red, Big Red, I got people in the office.' You have six minutes before Arnie's pickup comes up Main Street.

skillChecks.success: Dawn's knapsack: her Polaroid SX-70, her sketchbook, a Rockford library card, a bus schedule with MPLS circled, and a stack of Polaroids, the last of them dated in her hand '9/20 — so tired — so happy?', a frosted window with a clear round patch in it. (CLUE B5.) Gessler's bow case has a Wisconsin bowhunting license for 1973 and a note in his wallet: 'Russ — meet at the diner 6 a.m. — they say the rim is good for deer.'
skillChecks.failure: Too many bags, too little time, too much dust. You grab Dawn's knapsack and go.

scenes.name: The Hired Man's House
scenes.description: The Fossum place, after the co-op, or by day while Lillian is at church. Dawn, in the yellow-trimmed cardigan, on the step or asleep in a chair. She is pleased to see Ward ('Polecat!') and confused to see Tess. She is fine, she says, really, the people are so nice, she's staying for the festival. Bringing her back to herself is a process (see keyLocations): her real name and home and something only the two of them share, from Tess, gives her a WIS save DC 15 to want to go; Dr. Kubicek's 'tonic' poured out and a day without the town's bread gives another save with advantage; showing her the Polaroids from her own knapsack, or the tag on her knapsack in the back room, is the truth of it for her, a fear check DC 20, and an automatic success on wanting to leave, at a cost of 2 Dread and a long cry. Lillian Fossum, if present and handled kindly, does not stop them; she leaves the back door unlocked and walks out to the barn. But the dogs bark, and Arnie and his sons come up from evening milking, and the moment the party tries to put Dawn in a car, the hose across the step is the least of their worries: the Fork bridge, the road and the town are between Dawn and the water. Do not let the party drive her out this week. Arnie stands in the yard with his sons and four neighbours, unarmed, and says, very gently: 'She's not well. She's staying. You folks should go back to the motel now.' The town moves to Watchful, or to Closed. hs-scenario-003 begins.
scenes.readAloud: She is sitting on the step of the little white house in the last of the afternoon sun, in a cardigan too big for her, with her knees drawn up and a cigarette burning down between her fingers, and she is smiling at nothing. Long dark hair, a Rockford Central patch on the cardigan's pocket, a face that should be sharp and is soft, like someone who has just woken from a long sleep and would like to go back to it. When she sees you she lifts a hand. "Hey," she says. "Hey, you guys came for the festival. Isn't it nice here? Isn't everybody nice?" She looks at the cigarette as if she has forgotten how it got there. "I'm so tired all the time. Mrs. F says it's the country air." Behind her, through the screen door, there is a loaf of bread on the kitchen table, and frost on the inside of the bedroom window, in daylight, in the sun.

skillChecks.success: Dawn's pupils, her slowness, the bottle on the sill: Dr. Kubicek's 'tonic' is vitamins and phenobarbital, a small steady dose, enough to keep a young woman drowsy and calm. Pour it out and she will be clearer in a day. The rest of it, the contentment, is not in any bottle.
skillChecks.failure: She is very tired and a little feverish. Maybe it is the flu.

skillChecks.success: Something you say (her name, her mother's street, the song from the truck radio, the money she owes her sister) reaches her. She stops smiling, and looks at you as if she has just seen you, and says, very quietly, 'I want to go home. I don't know why I can't make myself want to go home.' She will go when you go.
skillChecks.failure: Dawn smiles and says she's staying for the festival, and asks if you'll come to the supper, and offers you a slice of bread.

skillChecks.success: Under the contentment, Dawn is terrified, and has been for weeks, and has no idea of what. Every night she wakes at three and the window is white.
skillChecks.failure: She seems happy. That is the worst thing about it.

encounters: Vernon Kittleson, the co-op night man (Night Watchman stats), who calls channel 14 before he fights
Arnie Fossum and four men in six minutes, unarmed, with flashlights and work gloves (Frightened Townsman stats, or Night Watchman for Arnie): they hold, tackle and shove, and do not punch first
A Rat Swarm in the co-op basement
At the Fossum yard, the two farm dogs (Feral Dog stats) and the whole family

npcsInvolved.name: Sheriff Clifford Dahlquist, 61
npcsInvolved.description: Heavy, grey, decent, tired, a year from his pension; eleven files in a bottom drawer.
npcsInvolved.motivation: He has looked, and wants it known that he has looked; he will act on evidence a jury would look at, and on nothing else.

npcsInvolved.name: Deputy Wes Garnett, 32
npcsInvolved.description: A farm boy from over the ridge, bowhunter, tan uniform, a spiral notebook with a list back to 1938, a cruiser with a radio.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Dr. Gessler left his bow in his trunk. No hunter does that.

npcsInvolved.name: Mrs. Jean Hovland, 64
npcsInvolved.description: Precise, cardiganed, county librarian since 1944, whose mother would not eat at a Hollow Fork table.

npcsInvolved.name: Dale Severson, 50
npcsInvolved.description: A quiet man who likes maps and was told to stop writing reports.
npcsInvolved.motivation: He would like to be proved right before he retires.

npcsInvolved.name: Einar Aldahl, 79
npcsInvolved.role: Head of the house of Aldahl, the family that left; Winona, Minnesota
npcsInvolved.description: Small, bald, bird-eyed, a cane and a temper; a hose across his step for twenty-three years.
npcsInvolved.motivation: He broke the bargain once and the town wrote two names the next year. He does not want to find out it was for nothing.

npcsInvolved.name: Ingeborg Vaage, 82
npcsInvolved.role: The last witness; tends the seventy stones
npcsInvolved.description: Pushing a mower round the stones on Wednesday and Sunday afternoons.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To see it end; she will tell everything in hs-scenario-003.

npcsInvolved.name: Rolf Haugen, 24
npcsInvolved.description: Little Elevator on channel 14; the safe combination; his father's heir, and the pen's.
npcsInvolved.motivation: He will not write a name. He would rather the town fell.

npcsInvolved.name: Harald Haugen, 58
npcsInvolved.role: The hand that writes the names
npcsInvolved.description: Found at his desk with the Book open in front of him, writing nothing.
npcsInvolved.motivation: He is waiting, without knowing it, for someone to make him stop.

npcsInvolved.name: Vernon Kittleson, 58
npcsInvolved.description: Thin, slow, a flashlight and a CB, a red kerchief, a bad back.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Do the job, call Arnie, don't get hurt, don't hurt anybody.

npcsInvolved.name: Dawn Petrakis, 22
npcsInvolved.description: Long dark hair, a too-big cardigan, Kools, a Polaroid camera, a sketchbook; sharp and funny under a month of bread and phenobarbital.
npcsInvolved.motivation: She wants to go home and cannot make herself want to.

npcsInvolved.name: Lillian Fossum, 46
npcsInvolved.description: Married in from Linden Falls in 1950; afraid every Labor Day.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Her boys; the guest's comfort; a prayer every night that the Hollow freezes solid.

npcsInvolved.name: Arnie Fossum, 49
npcsInvolved.description: Standing in his farmyard with his sons and neighbours, unarmed, asking the party to go back to the motel.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Four hundred acres, three sons, and a town.

rewards.money: Quentin's paper wires another $50 and wants the story by Friday the 11th. Deputy Garnett buys lunch at the Hardee's in Linden Falls. Photostats are ten cents a page in Madison and Linden Falls. A gallon of gas to Madison and back is about $6 a car. Anything taken from the co-op back room is evidence, and belongs to the families of the dead.
items: Rev. Caspar Penrose's Union Church register, 1878 to 1905 (CLUES 1d, 3b, 4b)
Polaroids or the original of every page of the Book (CLUES 4a, 1a, 2d), or the Book itself
Dawn's knapsack, Polaroid camera and Polaroids (CLUE B5)
Dr. Gessler's hunting license and his note to Russ, from the bow case
Photostats of the Courier and the Furrow for October 1904, and the overlay of the watershed and hail maps (CLUES 1b, 2b)
Einar Aldahl's red kerchief, and his telephone number

twists: The pencilled alternate is a player character: by default Russ Thorsen, who has eaten at Elsie's once a month for a year; otherwise whichever outsider has eaten most of the town's food. If Dawn is taken out of the watershed, Harald will strike her name and ink the alternate's, and the town's whole kindness turns on that character: they are fed, cared for, given a job, and watched.

Harald Haugen catches the party with the Book and lets them go. He does not tell the board. He does not tell Arnie. It is the first time in nineteen years he has not done what the Book asks, and he does not know why he did it.

Lillian Fossum was born in Linden Falls: she is an outsider who has eaten the town's bread for twenty-four years. She has been eligible every Labor Day of her married life, and she knows it. That is why she keeps the guests, and why, in the end, she may be the one who speaks for the house of Fossum.

The Furrow's microfilm in Madison exists because Gunnar Haugen, a careful man, promised the State Historical Society in 1903 to send every issue, and kept the promise long after the town would have wished he had not. The first writer of names left the evidence himself.
dmTips: This is the scenario in which the players learn the four rules. Every rule has three or more clues here (see conclusions), and core clues are found by looking in the right place, not by rolling. If the party skips Madison or Winona, the register and the Book between them still give every rule; if they skip the church, Einar and the Book carry it; if they cannot get into the co-op, Rolf brings them Polaroids of the Book on Saturday night.

Let the town react. By Wednesday the party is followed over the ridge; the sheriff tells them over the diner counter there is no case; Marit Lunde offers Quentin $500 for 'background research on the co-op's seventieth' to keep him busy; Arnie fixes Ward's air line and won't take money. The attitude is Watchful by Friday whatever the party does. Nobody threatens anybody. That is the frightening part.

The truth of it, the back room, is a DC 20 fear check (18 with Rule One known; the darkness adds 2 unless they have lights on). This is the scene to let a character break if the dice say so: they leave the co-op by the safest way and come back at Dread 4.

Rolf Haugen is the key to the Book, but not the only one. If the players do not trust him, Harald himself is the other: after the party has been in the church or to Winona, Harald sits in his office every night with the Book open, and a party that simply walks in and asks him will find a man who lets them read it.

Dawn does not leave this week. The party finds her, may begin to wake her, and learns that the town is between her and the water. Close the scenario with Arnie's gentle line in the farmyard and the town at Watchful or Closed.

Track the pull for every outsider who keeps eating the town's food. A character who has eaten Hollow Fork bread every day since 21 September is at DC 24 by Sunday 6 October. They should be finding the motel restful and the festival appealing, and the players should be noticing.
Budget an hour for Linden Falls (and two if they go to Madison), an hour for Winona and the church, an hour and a half for the co-op and Dawn.
